o: Delete one contiguous window from t so the rest of t is a subsequence of s, minimizing the window length. In Example 1 deleting just 'z' works (score 1); in Example 2 nothing of t appears in s, so we delete everything (score 3). With lengths up to 10⁵ we need near-linear time. Key structure: if we delete t[x..y], then t[0..x−1] must embed in a prefix of s and t[y+1..] in the complementary suffix.
k: pre[x] = shortest prefix length of s containing t[0..x−1]; suf[y] = shortest suffix length of s containing t[y..].
Window [x, y−1] is feasible iff pre[x] + suf[y] ≤ |s|.
As x grows, pre[x] is non-decreasing, so the minimal feasible y is non-decreasing — a two-pointer sweep works.

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix/suffix greedy matching + two pointers
a.i: Greedy matching gives pre and suf in linear time: scan s once left-to-right recording, for each prefix length of t, the shortest s-prefix that realizes it; scan right-to-left analogously for suffixes. Then slide x from 0 to m and advance y (the exclusive end of the deleted window) monotonically until pre[x] + suf[y] ≤ n; the answer is the minimum y − x seen. If t is already a subsequence of s, the answer is 0.
s: Compute pre[0..m] with a left-to-right greedy scan (INF if impossible).
Compute suf[0..m] with a right-to-left greedy scan.
Sweep x = 0..m; advance y (starting at 0, never decreasing, kept ≥ x) while y < m and pre[x] + suf[y] > n; track the minimum y − x.
a.t: O(n + m) — two greedy scans plus a two-pointer sweep
a.sp: O(m) — the pre and suf arrays

w: An alternative is binary search on the score with an O(m) feasibility check per step (O((n+m) log m)); the two-pointer version above is strictly better and just as simple once monotonicity is observed. Pitfalls: forgetting the score-0 case, mishandling INF when part of t cannot match at all, and letting y dip below x. Follow-up: report the actual window, not just its length.
